extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, editors, and advanced students of communication
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or operationalizing newsworthiness using the German/Galtung-Ruge derived list of news factors, interpreted through a cognitive-psychological lens. Useful for content analysis, editorial selection, and audience-attention studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: News factors as collective relevance indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: News factors are collective relevance indicators. They work because journalists use them to select, audiences use them to attend, and both use the same psychological mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat news factors not merely as editorial conventions but as signals of relevance that operate on both producers and consumers. Use this framing when designing content analyses or editorial selection policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that happen often or at regular intervals may be more likely to be covered; in content-analysis coding, mark repetition/regular occurrence as increasing newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale events passing a certain magnitude or intensity threshold qualify as newsworthy. Operationalize thresholds (e.g., death counts, economic impact) for consistent selection or coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that focus on individuals (heroes, victims, celebrities) are more recognizable and attract attention. In editing, emphasize human faces and narratives; in analysis, code for presence of individualized actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events involving high-status or elite actors (politicians, celebrities, corporate leaders) are privileged. Code for actor status and consider it a relevance multiplier in selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number and scope of people affected—geographic spread and demographic relevance—increase perceived social significance. Use geographic/demographic footprint as an operational variable in news selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consequences or impact of an event determine its newsworthiness. Evaluate probable effects and downstream consequences when deciding coverage or scoring stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy / Conflict
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict and controversy signal collective concern and draw attention. Code presence of dispute, disagreement, or polarizing elements; editors may prioritize such stories for audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggression
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of force or violent action increases salience. In content analyses, distinguish aggressive acts and note their weight in selection decisions; ethically consider sensationalism vs. public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material or social harm resulting from events makes them newsworthy. Measure damage (physical, economic, reputational) as part of impact/relevance coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful outcomes or victories (e.g., sporting wins, policy achievements) attract attention. Code positive outcome framing and recognize success as a distinct relevance signal from damage/aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected or novel events draw attention. Operationalize surprise by deviation from expectations or routine and treat it as a strong trigger for selection and audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing stories with previous coverage (continuity) maintain salience. Use story continuity as a factor in deciding follow-ups and allocating editorial resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involvement of institutions (government bodies, major organizations) increases newsworthiness. Code institutional actors separately from individuals and consider institutional ties when assessing significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors' power or ability to affect outcomes raises relevance. Assess actors' formal and informal influence as part of actor-coding schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnocentrism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories concerning one's own nation or in-group are privileged; when analyzing cross-national coverage, account for ethnocentric bias as a systematic factor influencing selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical relevance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree to which an event fits current topical themes or agendas affects coverage. Code alignment with ongoing public debates or dominant topics for use in content and audience studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary perspective (threat-detection bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans have learned more or less automatic reactions to stimuli that might be threatening; news factors like negativity, conflict, surprise tap evolved attention systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the evolutionary lens to explain why negativity, conflict, and surprise disproportionately capture attention. When designing experiments or interpreting audience responses, consider automatic threat-detection biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General psychological mechanisms (recognition/familiarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiar objects, persons, or events are recognized faster; mental matrices already exist for known entities. News factors like consonance, eliteness, personalization tap recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize familiarity/consonance in coding (e.g., known actors, familiar narratives). Recognize that recognizability speeds processing and increases selection likelihood for journalists and attention for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social relevance (collective concern signalling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach (number affected) signals social significance; controversy signals collective concern—audience attributes relevance to widely-relevant events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat measures of social scope and indicators of collective concern (e.g., public protests, widespread effects) as robust predictors of both editorial selection and audience interest.
